lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.unit_title: Creative Technology and AI Builder Lab
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus started Penalty Predictor and noticed that one direction was not behaving the way he expected.
lessons.course_context: Continue the same game entirely on the laptop. No paper Q&A.
learning_objectives: Add kick-history memory and a Keeper Brain.
Test one repeated pattern and one changed pattern.
Write one clear bug report and retest.
lessons.why_it_matters: Vibe coding means turning ideas into working products by describing, testing, fixing, and improving them.

vocabulary.definition: simple checks that tell you if a feature works
what you expected, what happened, how to repeat it, and how you will retest it

lessons.written_instruction: LAPTOP ONLY. Atticus: close the paper packet for this block. All Builder Lab questions, answers, plans, bug reports, and reflections happen in Smarticus and with your AI coding agent. Continue your current Penalty Predictor. Do not start over.

worked_examples.title: Game flow
worked_examples.problem: What should happen after a player chooses a direction?
worked_examples.solution: PLAYER CHOICE -> KEEPER CHOICE -> COMPARE -> GOAL or SAVE -> UPDATE SCORE.
worked_examples.explanation: A simple flow shows the behavior you want without needing code syntax.

guided_practice.prompt: On your laptop, finish five simple acceptance criteria. Ask Virgil to put them on the whiteboard as a checklist.

independent_practice.prompt: Fix LEFT/CENTER/RIGHT and goal/save behavior until all five checks pass.
Add kick-history memory and a visible Keeper Brain.
Test one repeated kick pattern and one changed pattern.
Write one bug report: What should happen? What happened instead? How can you repeat it? How will you test the fix?
If the main game works, add one fun upgrade.

exit_ticket.prompt: On your laptop, show the working game and explain in plain language how the Keeper Brain uses your earlier kicks.
exit_ticket.answer: The game remembers earlier choices, finds a pattern, and uses it to influence future keeper choices while keeping some randomness.

lessons.voice_prompt: LAPTOP ONLY. Never ask Atticus to write Builder Lab answers on paper. Keep all Q&A in Smarticus. Speak in short, age-appropriate sentences. If Atticus asks what a word means, explain it in plain language and return to the build. Ask simple questions such as: What do you want to happen? What happened instead? What should we test next? Proactively use whiteboard_draw for the game flow, a simple UI wireframe, the acceptance checklist, and a memory sketch: old kicks -> Keeper Brain -> next keeper guess. Use whiteboard_look if Atticus draws back. Do not teach code syntax unless he asks about a small snippet. If he asks what to prompt next, first ask what behavior he wants changed, then help turn that into one focused request plus one test.
